sales-report.text: Add a JSON sales reporting endpoint. Create Customer (name, email, country), Product (name, sku, price in cents, category), Order (customer, status: pending/paid/refunded, placed_at) and OrderItem (order, product, quantity, unit_price in cents) with migrations and factories. Add GET /api/reports/sales that accepts optional query params from, to (dates), country and status (default paid) and returns: total revenue, order count, average order value, revenue per country, top 5 products by revenue (name, sku, units, revenue) and the top 3 customers by spend. Money should be returned both as integer cents and as a formatted string. Invalid params must return 422.

blog-crud.text: Add a blog. Authenticated users can create, update, delete and list their own posts via a JSON API under /api/posts. A post has title, slug (generated from the title, unique), body, status (draft/published), published_at and belongs to a user; posts can have many tags (tags are created on the fly from an array of names). Only the author may update or delete a post (403 otherwise). Publishing a post (status -> published) sets published_at if missing. The index endpoint lists the current user's posts, newest first, filterable by status and tag, paginated, and includes tag names. Use Sanctum-style auth if available, otherwise the default auth guard with actingAs in tests.

csv-import.text: Add a product CSV import. POST /api/imports accepts an uploaded CSV file (max 5MB) with columns sku,name,price,stock. Store the file, create an Import record (user, status queued/processing/completed/failed, totals) and process it in the background: skip and record rows with invalid data (missing sku, non-numeric price, negative stock) with row number and reason, insert or update products by sku, then mark the import completed with counts (created, updated, failed) and email the user a summary. GET /api/imports/{import} returns status, counts and the list of row errors; only the owner may view it.

cart-discounts.text: Add cart pricing with discount codes. Model a Cart with CartItems (product name, unit price in cents, quantity, category) and DiscountCode (code, type: percentage/fixed/free_shipping, value, min_subtotal, applies_to_category nullable, expires_at, max_uses, times_used). POST /api/carts/{cart}/apply-discount with {code} validates the code (exists, not expired, under max uses, cart meets min subtotal) and returns a price breakdown: subtotal, discount, shipping (flat 4900 cents, free over 50000 cents subtotal or with free_shipping code), total, and per-line discounted prices. Category-restricted codes only discount matching lines. Return clear 422 errors for each failure reason.

blade-catalogue.focus: Blade: layouts/components, slots, @props/$attributes, directives (@error, @class, @selected...), old input, flash, pagination with query string, no logic/queries in views, redirect patterns
blade-catalogue.text: Add a server-rendered product catalogue using Blade (no SPA, no Livewire). Category (name, slug) and Product (category, name, slug, description, price in cents, stock, is_active). Public pages: /products lists active products with a text search, a category filter and a sort (newest, price asc/desc), paginated 12 per page with filters preserved across pages; /products/{slug} shows a product with an "Out of stock" badge when stock is 0 and a list of 4 related products from the same category. Admins (users with an is_admin boolean) get pages under /admin/products to create, edit and delete products using one shared form; validation errors appear next to each field, previously entered input is kept after a failed submit, and a success message is shown after saving. Use a shared layout and reusable view components. There is no frontend build available, so pages must render without compiled assets.

filament-admin.focus: Filament 5: resource structure (Schemas/Tables classes), form/table/filter/action APIs, enums with HasLabel/HasColor, relation managers, widgets, policies, eager loading, Filament testing helpers
filament-admin.text: The app has a Filament admin panel at /admin. Build a support-ticket admin in it. Customer (name, email, company), Ticket (customer, subject, body, status: open/pending/resolved, priority: low/normal/high/urgent, assigned agent = a User, nullable; resolved_at), TicketReply (ticket, author user, body, is_internal). Ticket resource: a table with searchable subject and customer name, sortable created date, status and priority shown as coloured badges, filters for status, priority, assignee and "unassigned only"; a create/edit form; a "Resolve" row action (sets status resolved and resolved_at) and a bulk "Assign to me" action; a replies relation manager on the ticket page. Add a Customer resource and a dashboard stats widget showing open tickets, urgent open tickets and the average resolution time in hours over the last 30 days. Only users with is_admin may delete tickets; any logged-in user may access the panel. Write Pest tests using Filament's testing helpers.

caching.focus: Caching: remember/flexible choice, key design, invalidation via model events, locks/stampede protection, stale fallback, Http client retries/timeouts, testing with Http::fake/travel
caching.text: Teams have Projects, and Projects have Tasks (title, status: open/done, completed_at, assignee user). Users belong to one team. Add GET /api/dashboard returning, for the current user's team: member count, project count, open task count, tasks completed in the last 7 days, and the top 5 projects by open tasks. It is expensive and hit constantly, so cache it per team; changes to that team's projects or tasks must be reflected within seconds, while serving slightly stale data for up to 5 minutes is acceptable if recomputing is slow. Also add GET /api/exchange-rates/{currency} (3-letter ISO code, validated) that returns rates from an external API at https://rates.example.test/latest?base={currency}. Cache the rates for one hour. When many requests miss at once, only one request may call the API. If the API is down or slow (over 3 seconds), return the last known rates with "stale": true, or 503 if there are none.

webhook-worker.focus: Queues/workers: idempotency, uniqueness/WithoutOverlapping, retries/backoff/ThrottlesExceptions, RateLimited middleware, failed(), afterCommit, queued notifications, pruning/scheduling, worker deployment config, Queue/Bus fakes
webhook-worker.text: Ingest payment-provider webhooks. POST /webhooks/payments receives JSON events {id, type, data} with an X-Signature header: HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body using a secret from configuration; invalid or missing signatures get 401. Store every event exactly once by its id (a duplicate delivery returns 200 and is not processed again) and respond quickly; process events in the background. Types: payment.succeeded (mark the Order paid and send the customer a receipt notification), payment.failed (mark the order payment_failed), refund.created (create a Refund and mark the order refunded). While processing, fetch payment details from the provider API GET https://api.payments.test/payments/{payment_id}; that API allows at most 10 requests per second and sometimes returns 5xx errors, so processing must retry with increasing delays, respect the limit, and never process the same event twice at the same time. Events that permanently fail must be marked failed with the error and be visible via GET /api/webhook-events?status=failed (admin only). Add a daily cleanup that deletes processed events older than 30 days. Document in the README how the queue workers must be run in production.

shipment-sync.focus: Background integration with an unreliable partner API: no duplicate shipments, nothing shipped for cancelled orders, transient errors retried without hammering the partner, permanent errors surfaced to ops, checkout stays fast
shipment-sync.text: Push paid orders to our warehouse partner. Create an Order model (soft-deletable, with a factory) with columns customer_email, shipping_address (text), total_cents, status (pending/paid), shipment_status (nullable: pending/sent/failed), shipment_reference (nullable) and shipment_failure_reason (nullable text). Add `Order::markAsPaid()`, which sets status paid in a database transaction and arranges for the shipment to be created in the background via a queued job `App\Jobs\SendOrderToWarehouse` that takes the order in its constructor. The job calls POST {services.warehouse.url}/shipments (default https://warehouse.example.test/api, bearer token services.warehouse.token) with the order id, address and total; a 201 returns {"id": "SHP-..."}, stored as shipment_reference with shipment_status sent. The partner allows 5 requests per second for our whole account, regularly answers 429 or 5xx for a minute or two and sometimes hangs. A 422 means the address is invalid: mark the shipment failed with the reason so ops can fix it by hand, without retrying. Orders cancelled (soft-deleted) before the job runs must never be shipped. Once the shipment exists, email the customer the mailable `App\Mail\ShipmentCreated` exactly once. If a shipment ultimately cannot be created, ops must see shipment_status failed and why.

statement-batch.focus: Fan-out background processing of many accounts: one broken account does not stop the rest, the run always reaches a final status with an accurate failure count, slow work kept off the default queue, request side stays fast, queue tables do not grow forever
statement-batch.text: Finance wants month-end statements. Create BillingAccount (name, email, active boolean; factory) and StatementRun (status: running/completed/completed_with_errors, total_accounts, failed_accounts default 0, completed_at nullable; factory). Add an invokable action `App\Actions\StartStatementRun` whose `__invoke(): StatementRun` creates a run (status running) and starts background processing for every active account, then returns immediately; production has about 40,000 active accounts. For each account, generate the PDF with the class `App\Services\StatementGenerator` (create it; `generate(BillingAccount $account): string` returning PDF bytes, a simple placeholder is fine), store it on the `local` disk at `statements/{run id}/{account id}.pdf`, then email the owner the mailable `App\Mail\StatementReady` (only after the file exists). PDF generation is slow and must not run on the default queue. One account failing (the generator throws) must not stop the others. When every account has been attempted, set the run to completed, or completed_with_errors with failed_accounts set to the number of accounts that failed, set completed_at, and email config('billing.finance_email') the mailable `App\Mail\StatementRunSummary`. We deploy on SQS with Redis as cache.

scheduled-reports.focus: Recurring tasks on several servers: each runs exactly once per occurrence at the intended local time, long or crashed runs cannot block or double up, large cleanups stay memory-safe, the schedule is tested
scheduled-reports.text: We run the shop on three app servers behind a load balancer; each runs the scheduler cron, and Redis is the shared cache and queue. The business runs on Copenhagen time. Add three recurring tasks. (1) Every Monday at 07:30 Copenhagen time, run a new command `reports:unshipped` that emails config('warehouse.email') the number of orders still unshipped 48 hours after being placed (create a minimal Order model: placed_at, shipped_at nullable). (2) Every night, run a new command `carts:prune-abandoned` that deletes carts not updated for 30 days (Cart model and factory, table `carts` with timestamps); there can be hundreds of thousands. (3) Every hour, dispatch a new queued job `App\Jobs\SyncSupplierStock` (no constructor arguments; a placeholder handle() that would call the supplier API is fine). It can take 20 to 40 minutes when the supplier is slow. Last quarter some tasks ran three times, and after a server was killed mid-run another task did not run again for a day; neither may happen. Add tests, and tell me how to check the schedule from the command line.

export-purge-command.focus: An operational command that deletes data: safe to run by hand against production, previewable, memory-safe on millions of rows, failures visible to automation through the exit code, safe to schedule on two servers
export-purge-command.text: Customers can request a CSV export of their data. Create an Export model with factory (table `exports`: id, user_id, path, timestamps); the files live on a new `exports` filesystem disk (local driver, root storage/app/exports). Add the console command `exports:purge` that deletes exports older than a retention period: the file and then the row. The retention is 30 days by default and can be changed with `--days=N`. The table has a few million rows in production. Support runs the command by hand against production when a customer complains, and wants to preview what would be removed with `--dry-run` (nothing is deleted then; print how many would be). In production the command must never delete anything unless the operator confirms it interactively or passes `--force` for unattended runs; when it refuses, it exits with a failure code. If a file cannot be deleted, keep its row so the next run retries it, carry on with the rest, and exit with a failure code so our automation notices. Print how many exports were removed. It must also run unattended every night at 03:00 on our two web servers (shared Redis cache), without overlapping a manual run. Write PHPUnit feature tests.

stock-sync-dispatcher.focus: A scheduled dispatcher feeding queued API work: every ready row is sent exactly once per change, abandoned work is picked up again, rate limits and API errors handled without loss, safe on several servers
stock-sync-dispatcher.text: Push stock allocations to our storefront. Create a StockAllocation model with factory (table `stock_allocations`: id, sku unique, quantity, sync_started_at nullable, synced_at nullable, disabled_at nullable, timestamps). A row is ready to sync when it is not disabled and has never been synced or was updated after its last sync. Add the command `stock:dispatch-sync`, scheduled every minute, which claims ready rows by setting sync_started_at and dispatches the queued job `App\Jobs\PushStockAllocations` in groups of at most 100; the job takes the list of row ids in its constructor and exposes it as the public property `$allocationIds`. A claim older than 15 minutes counts as abandoned and the row is ready again. The job sends POST https://storefront.example.test/api/stock with [{sku, quantity}, ...]; a 200 returns {"missing": [skus unknown to the storefront]}. Mark the sent rows synced (synced_at now, sync_started_at cleared) and set disabled_at on missing ones so they are not retried. The API is slow and returns 429 when we exceed its limit. If a job gives up for good, its rows must be picked up again by the next dispatcher run. Peak volume is about 5,000 ready rows; three containers run the scheduler, with Redis as the shared cache and SQS as the queue.

queue-bugfix.focus: Debugging existing background processing: find the root causes behind each symptom and fix them without breaking existing behaviour
queue-bugfix.text: Our app syncs newsletter subscribers to a CRM (see app/Jobs, app/Console/Commands, routes/console.php and the existing tests). Ops reported four problems. 1) When the CRM has an outage, affected subscribers never reach the CRM later, and nothing ever shows up in failed_jobs. 2) While the queue is backed up, the CRM receives the same subscriber many times. 3) After a container was killed during a deploy, the `crm:dispatch-sync` task did not run again for about a day. 4) The nightly `subscribers:normalize-emails` run leaves roughly half of the rows untouched each night. Find the root causes and fix them. Keep the existing behaviour and tests working, and add tests that prove each fix.

inactive-count.focus: A small read-only command and a schedule entry: correct, tested and proportionate to the need
inactive-count.text: Add a nullable last_login_at column to users. Add an Artisan command `users:inactive-count` that prints how many users have not logged in for the last N days (default 90, configurable with `--days`), counting users who never logged in as inactive. Run it once a day at 06:00 so the number shows up in our logs; we have a single server. Add tests.

coupon-redeem.focus: Concurrent writes: a per-user once rule and a hard cap that hold when requests for the same coupon race on several servers, side effects only for the request that actually created the redemption, correct API status codes
coupon-redeem.text: Add coupon redemption to our JSON API (Laravel Sanctum is installed; clients authenticate with bearer tokens). Create `App\Models\Coupon` (table `coupons`: `code` unique, `max_redemptions`, `redeemed_count` default 0) and `App\Models\CouponRedemption` (table `coupon_redemptions`: `coupon_id`, `user_id`, timestamps), with factories. `POST /api/coupons/{code}/redeem` is for authenticated users. An unknown code gets 404. Each user can redeem a coupon once: the first request returns 201, and repeating it returns 200 with the same redemption instead of creating another. Both return JSON `{"redemption_id": int, "redeemed_count": int}`. A coupon must never be redeemed more than `max_redemptions` times: once it is used up, other users get 409 with a `message`. Each new redemption dispatches the event `App\Events\CouponRedeemed` (its constructor takes the CouponRedemption) exactly once. We run several app servers on MySQL, and mobile clients retry and double-submit, so requests for the same coupon often arrive at the same moment.

orders-api.focus: An API for third-party integrations: correct authentication and authorization status codes and JSON bodies for every client, token abilities enforced, no data from other users, no internals in error responses
orders-api.text: Add an orders API for third-party integrations, authenticated with Sanctum personal access tokens (Sanctum is installed; integrations get tokens from `$user->createToken($name, $abilities)` and send them as a bearer token). Create `App\Models\Order` (table `orders`: `user_id`, `reference` unique, `total_cents`, timestamps) with a factory. Routes: `GET /api/orders` lists the token owner's orders, newest first, 20 per page; `GET /api/orders/{order}` shows one; `POST /api/orders` (`reference`, `total_cents` integer ≥ 1) creates one and returns 201. Reading needs the token ability `orders:read` and creating needs `orders:write`; a token without the ability gets 403. Nobody may see another user's order: answer 404 for it, the same as for an order that doesn't exist. Many integrations are scripts that send no `Accept` header, and they still need JSON responses with correct status codes. Production runs with APP_DEBUG off, and error responses must not reveal class names or other internals.

stock-csv-import.focus: Importing untrusted files: real-world CSVs from several systems accepted, bad rows reported precisely without blocking good ones, uploads validated, memory and file handles managed
stock-csv-import.text: Add a stock import to our API. `POST /api/stock-imports` (Sanctum-authenticated, multipart field `file`, a CSV of up to 5 MB) upserts rows into a `stock_levels` table (`sku` unique string, `quantity` unsigned integer, timestamps; model `App\Models\StockLevel`). Files come from several warehouse systems: the header row names the columns `sku` and `quantity` in any order and letter case, possibly with spaces around them, and a file may start with a UTF-8 byte-order mark and use CRLF or LF line endings. The delimiter is always a comma. Import the valid rows even when other rows are invalid. A row is invalid when it has the wrong number of columns, an empty sku, or a quantity that is not a whole number ≥ 0. Ignore blank lines. Respond 200 with JSON `{"imported": int, "errors": [{"line": int, "message": string}]}`, where `line` is the row's line number in the file (the header is line 1, and blank lines count). A file without both headers, or anything that is not a CSV file, gets 422. Importing a sku again updates its quantity.

document-vault.focus: Handling confidential uploads: only the allowed file types accepted, files stored safely and privately, download links that cannot be guessed, reused or kept, correct errors
document-vault.text: Add confidential document storage to our API (Sanctum is installed). `POST /api/documents` (multipart: `file` = a PDF, PNG or JPEG up to 5 MB; `title` = string up to 100 characters) stores the file and a `documents` row (`user_id`, `title`, `path`, `original_name`; model `App\Models\Document`) and returns 201 with `{"id": int}`. Documents are confidential and only their owner may get a download link. `GET /api/documents/{document}/link` returns `{"url": string}`: a link that downloads the file as an attachment without logging in (owners email it to their accountant) and stops working after 10 minutes. Another user asking for a link gets 404. If the stored file has gone missing, the link answers 404.

orders-customer-link.focus: Changing the schema of a large production table: zero-downtime release, correct foreign key behaviour, a safe and resumable backfill, indexes that fit the queries
orders-customer-link.text: This app runs in production on MySQL 8, and `orders` has 20 million rows. Orders point at customers only through `orders.customer_email`, which old checkouts stored without normalising (mixed case, spaces around it); `customers.email` is always lowercase and trimmed. Ship the first release of linking orders to customers by id. Add `orders.customer_id` referencing `customers`. Customers can be deleted (GDPR), and their orders must stay, detached from the customer. This release must deploy without downtime while the previous app version, which only knows `customer_email`, keeps running, so `customer_email` stays for now. `App\Actions\PlaceOrder` sets the new column as well. Add an Artisan command `orders:link-customers` that fills `customer_id` on existing orders by matching the email case-insensitively and ignoring spaces around it. It must be safe to re-run, leave orders whose email matches no customer untouched, and not change `updated_at` (our warehouse sync reads it). Switch `GET /api/customers/{customer}/orders?status=` to the new column. That endpoint is called very often, so make sure the database can answer it efficiently.

carrier-quote.focus: Calling an unreliable partner API from a request: bounded time, retries only where they help, clean error mapping, a fallback, configuration and tests without real network calls
carrier-quote.text: Add shipping quotes from our carrier. `GET /api/shipping/quotes?postcode=XXXX` (public; the postcode is 4 digits, anything else gets 422) returns `{"estimated": false, "rates": [{"service": string, "price_cents": int}]}` from the carrier, through a class `App\Services\CarrierClient` with a method `quote(string $postcode): array` that returns the rates. Its configuration lives in `config/services.php` under `carrier`: `base_url` (default https://carrier.example.test), `key`, and `fallback_cents` (default 995). The carrier's API is `GET {base_url}/v2/rates?postcode=...` with the key as a bearer token, and it returns `{"rates": [...]}` in the same shape. For an unknown postcode it answers 404: respond 422 with a `message`. The carrier is flaky: it sometimes answers 5xx or hangs. Our checkout calls this endpoint and must get an answer within 5 seconds. Call the carrier at most 3 times in total per quote, and if it still fails, respond 200 with `{"estimated": true, "rates": [{"service": "standard", "price_cents": <fallback_cents>}]}`. A 401 from the carrier means our key is wrong: don't retry it, report the error so we get alerted, and serve the fallback.

ship-order.focus: Side effects of a state change: email and points exactly once, nothing when the surrounding transaction rolls back, no double shipping under concurrent requests, testable mail
ship-order.text: Staff ship orders through our API (Sanctum is installed). Add a boolean `users.is_staff` (default false) and an unsigned integer `users.points` (default 0). Create `App\Models\Order` (`user_id` = the customer, `status` pending/paid/shipped, `total_cents`) and `App\Models\OrderShipment` (table `order_shipments`: `order_id` unique, `carrier`, `tracking_number`, timestamps), with factories. Add `Order::ship(string $carrier, string $trackingNumber): OrderShipment`. It marks the order shipped, records the shipment, emails the customer the mailable `App\Mail\OrderShipped` (which shows the tracking number), and adds `total_cents / 100` points (rounded down) to the customer. `POST /api/orders/{order}/ship` (body: `carrier`, `tracking_number`) calls it and returns 201. Only staff may call it (others get 403). An order that is already shipped gets 409, and nothing happens again. Back-office tools often call `ship()` inside larger database transactions. If such a transaction rolls back, the customer must not get an email and no points may be added.

token-login.focus: Issuing and revoking API tokens: correct status codes and JSON bodies for every client, brute-force protection that cannot be bypassed or that blocks the wrong people, no secrets in responses
token-login.text: Add token login for our mobile app (Sanctum is installed). `POST /api/auth/token` (public; `email`, `password`, `device_name`) returns 201 with `{"token": string}`, a Sanctum personal access token, for valid credentials. A missing field gets 422 with validation errors, and a wrong email or password gets 401 with `{"message": "Invalid credentials."}`. To slow down password guessing, allow at most 5 attempts per minute for the same email from the same IP address; further attempts get 429. `DELETE /api/auth/token` (authenticated) revokes the token used for that request and returns 204. `GET /api/me` (authenticated) returns the user's `id`, `name` and `email`.

thread-mentions.focus: Notifications triggered by a write: the right people notified exactly once each, private emails, nothing sent when the write fails, counters kept correct, tests that prove it
thread-mentions.text: Add replies with @mentions to discussion threads in our API (Sanctum is installed). Users get a unique, lowercase `username` column (add it, and to the user factory). Create `App\Models\Thread` (`user_id`, `title`, `reply_count` default 0) and `App\Models\Reply` (`thread_id`, `user_id`, `body`), with factories. `POST /api/threads/{thread}/replies` (authenticated; `body` = required string up to 2000 characters) creates a reply, increments `threads.reply_count` and returns 201 with `{"id": int}`. Every distinct `@username` in the body (matched case-insensitively) that names an existing user other than the reply's author gets one email, the mailable `App\Mail\MentionedInReply`, addressed only to them, and one database notification, `App\Notifications\MentionedInReply`, stored in the standard `notifications` table. Unknown usernames are ignored. If storing the reply fails, nobody is emailed or notified.

profile-nickname.focus: A small profile endpoint: correct, tested and proportionate to the need
profile-nickname.text: Add a nullable `nickname` column (at most 30 characters) to users. `GET /api/me` returns the authenticated user's `id`, `name` and `nickname`, and `PATCH /api/me` sets or clears the nickname. Both use Sanctum authentication (installed).

acme-webhooks.focus: Receiving signed provider webhooks: the signature checked over exactly the bytes received and failing closed, the endpoint reachable by the provider, a fast acknowledgement with the slow work done in the background and retried, every event applied once despite duplicates and redeliveries, out-of-order events never overwriting newer state, unknown event types acknowledged
acme-webhooks.text:
Receive payment webhooks from our payment provider, Acme Pay. Acme sends `POST /webhooks/acme` with a JSON body `{"id": "evt_...", "type": string, "occurred_at": ISO-8601 UTC timestamp, "data": object}` and an `Acme-Signature` header: the base64-encoded HMAC-SHA256 of the request body, keyed with the signing secret in `config('services.acme.webhook_secret')`. A request whose signature is missing or wrong gets 401 and must change nothing. The event types we handle are:
- `payment.succeeded`, with `data` = `{"payment_id": string, "amount": integer in minor units, "currency": string}`: the payment is succeeded and the ledger gets an entry of `+amount`;
- `payment.refunded`, with the same `data`: the payment is refunded and the ledger gets an entry of `-amount`.
Acme sends other event types too, and adds new ones over time; acknowledge those and ignore them.
Keep payments in a `payments` table (`acme_id` unique, `status` = `succeeded` or `refunded`, `card_last4`, plus anything else you need) and ledger entries in a `ledger_entries` table (`payment_id` = the Acme payment id, `amount` = signed integer in minor units, plus anything else you need). To get `card_last4`, fetch the payment from Acme's API, `GET https://api.acmepay.test/v1/payments/{payment_id}` with the key in `config('services.acme.api_key')` as a bearer token; it returns the payment's current state, `{"id", "status", "amount", "currency", "card_last4"}`.
How Acme behaves in production: it waits at most 5 seconds for a 2xx response and otherwise retries the delivery for up to 24 hours. It also delivers the same event more than once, sometimes hours apart, and in any order. A payment's status must reflect its newest event by `occurred_at`, and each event must reach the ledger exactly once. Acme's API is sometimes slow or down for minutes, and the work must still happen once it is back. We run several app servers on MySQL, and every deploy clears the application cache.

notes-search-api.focus: A team-scoped search API that treats every query parameter and body field as hostile: sorting limited to the public fields, search terms matched literally, no access to another team's projects or notes, and internal columns never returned or usable through the API
notes-search-api.text: Add a team notes API (Sanctum is installed; clients send bearer tokens). Users belong to a team: add `team_id` to `users`. Create `App\Models\Team` (table `teams`: `name`), `App\Models\Project` (table `projects`: `team_id`, `name`, `secret` nullable) and `App\Models\Note` (table `notes`: `team_id`, `project_id`, `user_id` for the author, `title`, `body`, `secret` nullable, `api_token` nullable, timestamps), each with a factory. `secret` and `api_token` are internal columns used by other systems: the API must never return them, and they must not be usable to sort or filter results. All routes are for authenticated users and only ever touch the user's own team. `GET /api/notes?sort=&dir=&q=&per_page=` lists the team's notes, paginated (`per_page` default 20, at most 100) with the notes under `data`. The list can be sorted by `title` or `created_at` only, `dir` is `asc` or `desc`, and the default is newest first. `q` searches note titles: a title matches when it contains the term literally, because users search for things like `100%` and `a_b`. `POST /api/notes` (`project_id`, `title` up to 200 characters, `body`) creates a note in one of the team's projects, with the user as author, and returns 201. `GET /api/notes/{note}` shows one note. Every note in a response has `id`, `title`, `body`, `created_at`, `project` (`id`, `name`) and `author` (`id`, `name`). The API is public to our customers' integrations, so expect crafted query strings and request bodies. Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8.

livewire-notes.focus: Livewire pages that treat the browser as untrusted: only the owner can read, change or delete a note however the page state or requests are tampered with, input validated before every write, and list queries that stay flat as the number of rows grows on every request, not only the first
livewire-notes.text:
Add personal notes pages to this app with Livewire (livewire/livewire 4 is installed; full-page components render in `resources/views/layouts/app.blade.php`). Do not install Flux, Filament, Fortify or a starter kit. Sign-in is handled elsewhere: tests use `actingAs`, and a stub `login` route exists. Production runs on several servers on MySQL. Users keep thousands of notes, some notes have hundreds of comments, and our security team tests every page with the browser's developer tools open.

Create `App\Models\Note` (table `notes`: `user_id` = the owner, `title`, `body`, timestamps) and `App\Models\Comment` (table `comments`: `note_id`, `user_id` = the commenter, `body`, timestamps), with factories. Comments are written by another part of the product, so they need no UI here.

All pages are for signed-in users only (guests are redirected to `login`). Users see and change only their own notes.
- `GET /notes`, route name `notes.index`, Livewire component `notes.index`: the current user's notes, newest first (by `created_at`), 10 per page, with the page number in the URL as `?page=`. Each row shows the note's title, its number of comments as `{n} comments`, and the name of the user who wrote its most recent comment (nothing when it has no comments). The component's `search` property filters the list to notes whose title contains the text, ignoring case; changing the search goes back to the first page. Each row has a delete button that calls the component's `delete` action with the note's id.
- `GET /notes/create`, route name `notes.create`, component `notes.create`: the form fields are the component properties `title` and `body`; the `save` action creates the note for the current user and redirects to `notes.index`.
- `GET /notes/{note}/edit`, route name `notes.edit`, component `notes.edit`, which receives the note as the mount parameter `note`: properties `title` and `body` start with the note's values; `save` updates the note, and `delete` deletes it and redirects to `notes.index`.

If you prefer a form object, expose it as the property `form` (so the fields are `form.title` and `form.body`). Validation: `title` is required, 3 to 100 characters; `body` is required, at most 5000 characters. Invalid input shows errors next to the fields and changes nothing.

inertia-projects.focus: Server side of Inertia pages for another team's React front end (no JavaScript is expected): nothing beyond what the pages need reaches the browser in page or shared props, neither account secrets on users nor internal project fields; prop shapes exactly as the pages read them; the large activity list loaded only when the page asks for it; validation errors returned the way Inertia forms expect; owner-only access
inertia-projects.text:
Add the server side of the project tracker to this Inertia app (inertia-laravel 3 is installed and its middleware is registered). The React pages belong to the front-end team, who build them against the props described here, so deliver routes, controllers, policies, props and tests only: do not write JavaScript or page components, and do not run npm.

Already in the app, with factories: `App\Models\Project` (table `projects`: `user_id` (the owner), `title`, `description` nullable, `status` (`draft`, `active` or `archived`), and `internal_notes` and `internal_cost_cents`, which only the finance team reads, in another system) and `App\Models\AuditEntry` (table `audit_entries`: `project_id`, `message`, timestamps; `Project::auditEntries()`). The `users` table also has two-factor and billing columns that other features maintain. Sign-in is handled elsewhere: tests use `actingAs`, and a stub `login` route exists.

Everything below needs a signed-in user. Users see and change only their own projects, and another user's project must be refused.
- `GET /projects` (`projects.index`) renders the component `Projects/Index`. Prop `projects`: the user's projects, newest first, 20 per page. The page reads the list from `projects.data` (each item `{ id, title, status }`) and the pagination links that come with it.
- `POST /projects` (`projects.store`): `title` required, at most 120 characters; `description` optional; `status` one of the three values. It creates the project for the current user and redirects to its `projects.show` page.
- `GET /projects/{project}` (`projects.show`) renders `Projects/Show`. Prop `project`: the page reads `project.id`, `project.title`, `project.description` and `project.status`. Prop `activity`: the project's 20 newest audit entries, newest first, each `{ id, message, created_at }` (the page reads `activity[0].message`). The audit table is very large. The activity panel is collapsed when the page opens, and the page asks for `activity` with a partial reload only when the user expands it, so activity must not be queried when the page opens or on any other partial reload (after an inline title edit the page reloads only `project`).
- `PUT /projects/{project}` (`projects.update`) takes the same fields and rules and redirects to `projects.show`.
- `DELETE /projects/{project}` (`projects.destroy`) redirects to `projects.index`.

Every page also gets a shared prop `auth.user`, which the header reads: `{ id, name, email }`, with only those keys, for the signed-in user, and `null` for a guest. The forms are Inertia forms (`useForm`) and show validation errors next to each field.

payments-errors.focus: Honest error reporting around a payment gateway: expected declines stay quiet, an outage is visible once at the agreed severity with enough detail to debug, real bugs are reported as errors, and nothing sensitive or internal leaks into responses or logs
payments-errors.text: Add card payments to our JSON API (Sanctum is installed; clients send bearer tokens). `POST /api/payments` (authenticated; `amount` integer of at least 1, in minor units; `currency` a three-letter code; `card_token` the string our payment form gets from the card vault) charges the card and returns 201 with `{"reference": string}`, the gateway's reference. Talk to the gateway only through the interface `App\Contracts\PaymentGateway`, which has one method, `public function charge(int $amount, string $currency, string $cardToken): string`, returning the reference. Another team is writing the real client, so bind a placeholder implementation for now; tests swap in their own. The gateway signals two failures by throwing exceptions that you create: `App\Exceptions\CardDeclined` and `App\Exceptions\GatewayUnavailable`, each constructed with just a message (`new CardDeclined('...')`). A declined card is a normal outcome for a shop: answer 402 with `{"error": "card_declined"}`, and it must not alert anyone. A gateway outage is not a bug in our code, but ops must see it: answer 503 with `{"error": "gateway_unavailable"}`, and record it once per failed payment at `warning` level, which ops watch separately from errors. Anything else that goes wrong is a bug and must be reported like any other error (answer 500 or 503) without revealing internals to the client. Every failure is investigated from the logs and our error tracker, so what gets recorded must be enough to debug it. Card tokens are sensitive and must never appear in logs or error reports. Production runs with APP_DEBUG off.

invoice-totals.focus: Invoice money handled exactly: amounts parsed without loss, each currency's decimal places respected, VAT, discounts and instalments that add up to the cent, and money in responses that clients can trust
invoice-totals.text:
Add invoices to our shop's API. Invoices are sent to accounting software that rejects any invoice whose amounts don't add up to the cent. No authentication is needed for these endpoints. We sell in EUR, DKK and JPY today. We will add currencies with three decimal places (such as KWD) later, and that should not need changes to the calculation code.

`POST /api/invoices` takes `{"currency": "EUR", "vat_rate": 25, "discount": "1.00", "lines": [{"sku": "A-1", "unit_price": "19.99", "quantity": 3}]}`. `currency` is one of EUR, DKK or JPY. `vat_rate` is a whole percentage from 0 to 100. `lines` has at least one line, and `quantity` is a whole number of at least 1. `discount` is optional. Prices and the discount are strings in major units, written as digits with an optional `.` and fraction (`"19.99"`, `"0.5"`, `"150"`), with no more decimal places than the currency has: two for EUR and DKK, none for JPY. Any other value is rejected with 422 and nothing is stored. A discount larger than the sum of the lines is also a 422.

A valid request stores the invoice in an `invoices` table and returns 201 with the invoice. Every money amount in a response is an integer number of minor units (cents for EUR, øre for DKK, yen for JPY), never a float or a string. The invoice JSON has `id`, `currency`, `vat_rate`, `subtotal_minor`, `discount_minor`, `net_minor`, `vat_minor`, `gross_minor` and `lines`. The lines are in the order they were sent, and each has `sku`, `quantity`, `unit_price_minor`, `subtotal_minor` (unit price × quantity), `discount_minor`, `net_minor` (subtotal − discount), `vat_minor` and `gross_minor` (net + VAT).

Finance has fixed the calculation rules:
- The invoice discount is spread over the lines in proportion to their subtotals, and the line discounts add up to the invoice discount.
- VAT is calculated per line on the line's net amount, rounded to the nearest minor unit, with halves rounded up.
- Each invoice amount (`subtotal_minor`, `discount_minor`, `net_minor`, `vat_minor`, `gross_minor`) is the sum of that amount over the lines.

`GET /api/invoices/{id}` returns the same invoice JSON. `POST /api/invoices/{id}/split` with `{"parts": 3}` (2 to 12) splits the invoice's gross amount into that many instalments for a payment plan, as equal as possible, and returns 200 with `{"parts_minor": [...]}`.

team-invitations.focus: Invitation tokens handled like passwords: never recoverable from the database, logs or responses, single use, guessing limited per email and IP without locking out other people, and no redirect off our site after accepting
team-invitations.text:
Add team invitations (Laravel Sanctum is installed; API clients authenticate with bearer tokens). Create a `teams` table (`id`, `name`, `owner_id` referencing users, timestamps) and a `team_user` table for members (`team_id`, `user_id`, each pair at most once); our tests insert teams directly into `teams`. `App\Models\User` and its factory already exist.
- `POST /api/teams/{team}/invitations`, JSON `{"email": string}`: only the team's owner may invite; anyone else gets 403. The email must belong to a registered user (422 otherwise). Store the invitation in an `invitations` table (`team_id`, `email`, plus whatever else you need), answer 201 with JSON `{"id": int, "email": string}`, and email the invitee a link to `/invitations/accept?token=<token>` on our site, where the token is a new secret, random value.
- `POST /invitations/accept` is the form post from the page that link opens (that page is built by our front-end team; you only build the POST). The invitee is not logged in. Form fields: `email` and `token`; the query string may carry `return_to`. If the token belongs to a not yet accepted invitation for that email, the user with that email joins the team, and the browser is redirected to `return_to` when it is a path on our own site, otherwise to `/teams/{team_id}`. Each invitation can be accepted only once. A wrong email or token adds nobody.
The token is as good as a password for joining the team: it must never be readable from our database, our logs or any API response. To make guessing impractical, allow at most 5 accept attempts per minute for the same email from the same IP address; further attempts get 429. Whole departments often accept their invitations from one office IP address, and we run several app servers.

partner-sync.focus: An unattended sync command against a flaky partner: every failure is visible to ops with enough detail to debug it, an outage does not flood the error tracker, one bad record never stops the rest, automation sees failures through the exit code, and the load balancer stops routing to a server that cannot reach its database without health checks restarting servers during a database blip
partner-sync.text: We push product data to a retail partner. Add the interface `App\Contracts\PartnerApi` with one method, `push(string $id): void`, which sends one product to the partner and throws `App\Exceptions\PartnerDown` (constructed as `new PartnerDown(string $message)`) when the partner is unavailable. Implement it over HTTP: `POST {services.partner.url}/products/{id}`; a connection failure or a 5xx answer means the partner is down. Add the console command `partner:sync {ids*}` that pushes each given id. It runs unattended from the scheduler on our servers, and nobody watches its output. A failure for one id, whatever its cause, must never stop the remaining ids, and every failure must reach our error tracker (it is fed from the application's error reporting and logs) with enough detail for a developer to debug it. The command exits with a non-zero code if any id failed, so our job monitor raises an alert. When the partner has an outage, every id fails with the same error, and last month that buried the error tracker in thousands of identical entries. Ops still want to see an outage, but no more than 3 entries per minute for the same kind of error. Separately, our load balancer checks `GET /up` on each server: it must fail (a 5xx answer) when that server cannot reach its database, so traffic stops going there, and succeed otherwise. Our container platform also needs a liveness URL, `GET /live`, which restarts a server when it fails; it must not depend on the database, so a database blip never restarts every server at once. Production runs several servers on MySQL with a shared Redis cache.

subscription-renewals.focus: Dates and times that are right for every customer: renewal dates that follow the start date through short months and leap years, a 'today' that is the customer's own calendar day, and timestamps that identify the real moment
subscription-renewals.text:
Our customers are in New Zealand, Europe and the US, and support gets tickets about orders missing from the customer's "today" screen and renewal dates that drift. Add the following to our API. It is an internal service behind our gateway, so these endpoints need no authentication.

Users get a `timezone` column with an IANA timezone name such as `Europe/Copenhagen` (default `UTC`). `PATCH /api/users/{user}` with `{"timezone": "America/New_York"}` changes it and returns 200. A value that is not a known IANA timezone name is rejected with 422 and the user is not changed.

`POST /api/users/{user}/subscriptions` with `{"started_on": "2026-01-31"}` (a calendar date) creates a monthly subscription and returns 201 with `{"id", "user_id", "started_on", "renews_on", "created_at"}`. Its first renewal date is one month after `started_on`. `POST /api/subscriptions/{subscription}/renew` records that the current period is paid, moves `renews_on` to the next renewal date and returns 200 with the same JSON. Renewal dates are always calculated from the start date: the nth renewal is n months after `started_on`, on the same day of the month, or on the last day of the month when that month is shorter. So a subscription started on 2026-01-31 renews on 2026-02-28, then 2026-03-31, then 2026-04-30, and one started on 2024-01-31 first renews on 2024-02-29. `started_on` and `renews_on` are written `YYYY-MM-DD` in JSON.

`POST /api/users/{user}/orders` with `{"reference": "A-100"}` records an order placed at the current moment and returns 201 with `{"id", "reference", "placed_at"}`. `GET /api/users/{user}/orders/today` returns `{"data": [...]}` with that user's orders, in the same shape, that were placed during the current calendar day in the user's own timezone.

Timestamps in JSON (`placed_at`, `created_at`) are ISO-8601 instants in UTC.

team-activity.focus: A small internal read-only page: correct, tested and proportionate to the need
team-activity.text: Add an internal admin page at `GET /admin/team`, a plain server-rendered Blade page for our staff (every user of this app is staff; there are about 40 and no roles). It lists every user with their name and when they last signed in, as relative text such as `3 minutes ago` or `2 days ago`, or `never` if they have not signed in yet. Above the list it shows `Active in the last 7 days: N`, where N is the number of users whose last sign-in falls on today or one of the six days before it, going by the calendar in Copenhagen, where the whole team works. Add a nullable `last_login_at` column to users and keep it up to date whenever a user signs in through Laravel's standard authentication. Guests must not see the page: send them to `/login` (another team is building the login page there). The app and its database keep timestamps in UTC.

team-permissions.focus: Per-team authorization with a roles package: a role in one team never grants anything in another team, members without a role only read, what a role allows comes from its granted permissions and a change applies on the next request, and the role setup can be re-run on every deploy without errors or duplicates
team-permissions.text:
Add team posts with per-team roles. Laravel Sanctum is installed (API clients send bearer tokens), and we use spatie/laravel-permission for roles and permissions: it is installed and its config and migration are published, but nothing in the app uses it yet. Change its config or migration if you need to.
Create `App\Models\Team` (table `teams`: `name`, timestamps) and `App\Models\Post` (table `posts`: `team_id`, `user_id` for the author, `title`, `body`, timestamps), each with a factory; our tests create posts with `Post::factory()->create(['team_id' => ..., 'user_id' => ...])`. Add `Team::addMember(User $user, ?string $role = null): void`, which makes the user a member of the team with the role `admin`, the role `editor`, or no role. A user can belong to several teams and have a different role in each.
What each role may do in its own team: any member may list the team's posts; an editor may also create posts and update any post; an admin may also delete posts. A member without a role only reads. Nobody can see or touch posts of a team they don't belong to.
Which actions a role allows must come from the permissions granted to that role, not from checks on the role's name: operations will grant and revoke permissions on roles at runtime with the package's own methods, and a change must apply from the very next request on every app server. Create the roles and permissions in `Database\Seeders\RolesAndPermissionsSeeder` and call it from `DatabaseSeeder`. Deploys run the seeder every time, so it must be safe to run again and again.
Routes, all for authenticated users:
- `GET /api/teams/{team}/posts` lists the team's posts, with the posts under `data`.
- `POST /api/teams/{team}/posts` (`title` up to 200 characters, `body`) creates a post in that team with the user as author and returns 201.
- `PATCH /api/posts/{post}` (`title`, `body`) updates a post.
- `DELETE /api/posts/{post}` deletes a post.
Each post in a response has `id`, `team_id`, `title`, `body` and `author` (`id`, `name`). Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8 behind several app servers sharing a Redis cache.

shipments-api.focus: A warehouse-scoped list and create API that treats every query parameter and body field as hostile: filters that match values exactly (an id never matches a longer id, a status never matches a longer status, a false flag finds the false rows), unknown or internal filters and sorts refused as a client error, no rows from other or missing warehouses, and a carrier id accepted only when it is a well-formed id of a carrier in the user's own warehouse
shipments-api.text:
Add a warehouse shipments API (Sanctum is installed; clients send bearer tokens). Our team uses spatie/laravel-query-builder for list endpoints, so list query strings follow its conventions: `filter[<name>]=<value>`, `sort=<field>` for ascending and `sort=-<field>` for descending. Create a `warehouses` table (`name`, timestamps), add a nullable `warehouse_id` to `users`, and create a `carriers` table (`warehouse_id` nullable, `name`, timestamps) and a `shipments` table (`warehouse_id` nullable, `user_id` for the user who created it, `carrier_id`, `code`, `status` stored as the plain string `unpaid`, `paid` or `shipped`, `paid` boolean, `label_secret` nullable, timestamps), with models `App\Models\Warehouse`, `App\Models\Carrier` and `App\Models\Shipment`. Our tests insert warehouses, carriers and shipments directly into these tables, so any other column you add must be nullable or have a default. `label_secret` is used by the label printer: the API must never return it, and it must not be usable to filter or sort. Both routes are for authenticated users and only ever touch the user's own warehouse. Some staff have no warehouse yet (`warehouse_id` null), and some old shipments and carriers have no warehouse either; those belong to nobody and must not reach anyone through the API.
- `GET /api/shipments` lists the warehouse's shipments, newest first, 20 per page, with the shipments under `data`. Filters: `user_id` (shipments created by that user), `status` (one of the three statuses), `paid` (`1`/`true` or `0`/`false`). Sorts: `code`, `status`, `created_at`. Any other filter or sort is a client error (400 or 422), never a server error.
- `POST /api/shipments`, JSON `{"carrier_id": int, "code": string up to 32 characters}`, creates a shipment in the user's warehouse with the user as creator, status `unpaid` and `paid` false, and returns 201 with the shipment. The carrier must be one of the user's warehouse's carriers; invalid input gets 422.
Each shipment in a response has `id`, `code`, `status`, `paid`, `user_id`, `carrier_id` and `created_at`. The API is used by our customers' integrations, so expect crafted query strings and request bodies. Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8.

profile-patch.focus: Request and response objects that treat input as hostile and partial: a field left out keeps its value while an explicit null clears it, privileged columns can never be set from a request or an import row, invalid input is rejected before anything is written, related posts are only loaded when asked for, and a messy import skips bad rows while still importing good ones and reporting failure
profile-patch.text:
Add a profile API for the signed-in user and a profile import command. Sanctum is installed; API clients send bearer tokens. The team uses spatie/laravel-data for request and response objects.
Add to `users`: `bio` (nullable, up to 500 characters), `phone` (nullable, up to 30 characters), `is_admin` (boolean, default false) and `team_id` (nullable integer; teams live in another service, so no foreign key). Only our admin tools set `is_admin` and `team_id`. Create `App\Models\Post` (table `posts`: `user_id`, `title`, timestamps) with a factory, and a user's posts relation.
- `GET /api/profile` returns 200 with the profile as a JSON object, not wrapped in a `data` key: `{"id": int, "name": string, "email": string, "bio": string|null, "phone": string|null}`. With `?include=posts` it also has `"posts": [{"id": int, "title": string}]`, the user's own posts. Without it there is no `posts` key, and since some users have thousands of posts, the posts must not be loaded at all.
- `PATCH /api/profile` updates any of `name` (string, up to 100 characters, cannot be cleared), `email` (a valid email address, unique among users), `bio` and `phone`, and returns 200 with the profile in the same shape (no `posts`). Clients send only the fields they change: a field left out of the body keeps its stored value, and `bio` or `phone` sent as `null` clears it. Invalid input gets 422 and changes nothing. Nothing else about the user can be changed through this endpoint, whatever the body contains.
- `php artisan profiles:import {path}` reads a JSON file holding an array of rows, each an object with `email`, `name` and optionally `bio` and `phone`, under the same rules as PATCH. A row whose email matches an existing user updates that user; otherwise it creates one with a random password. The export is messy: a row breaking the rules is skipped and reported with its position and writes nothing, and the valid rows are still imported. The command exits 0 when every row was imported and non-zero when any row was rejected or the file is missing or unreadable. Rows sometimes carry other columns such as `is_admin`; they must have no effect.
Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8.

payment-states.focus: Payment state changes that happen exactly once under double submits and concurrent requests holding stale copies, side effects such as the ledger entry and the receipt email only when the change is committed, only the allowed forward moves, and untrusted state names rejected cleanly instead of crashing
payment-states.text:
Add payments to the API (Sanctum is installed; clients send bearer tokens). Our team models state machines with spatie/laravel-model-states, which is installed; use it for the payment's state. Create `App\Models\Payment` (table `payments`: `user_id` referencing users, `amount` integer in minor units, `currency` 3-letter code, `state`). `state` is stored in the database as `pending`, `paid` or `refunded`, and a new payment is `pending`. Our tests insert rows into `payments` directly with only those four columns and read `state` back, so any other column must be nullable or have a default. Keep ledger entries in a `ledger_entries` table (`payment_id`, `amount` = signed integer in minor units, plus anything else you need). Add a boolean `is_admin` column to `users`, default false.
- `POST /api/payments/{payment}/pay`: only the payment's own user (403 for anyone else). A pending payment becomes paid, the ledger gets one entry of `+amount`, and the user is emailed a receipt. Answers 200 with the payment.
- `POST /api/payments/{payment}/refund`: admins only (403 otherwise). A paid payment becomes refunded and the ledger gets one entry of `-amount`. Answers 200 with the payment.
- `PUT /api/admin/payments/{payment}/state`, JSON `{"state": string}`: admins only (403 otherwise), for support staff correcting mistakes. Sets the payment to the named state whatever its current state, with no ledger entry and no email, and answers 200. A name that is not one of the three states gets 422 and changes nothing. The name comes from a free-text field in the support tool, so expect typos and junk.
Pay and refund only move forward: pending to paid, and paid to refunded. Any other pay or refund gets 409 or 422 and changes nothing. A payment is paid at most once, with one ledger entry and one receipt, even when the mobile app double-submits or two pay requests for the same payment reach two of our app servers at the same moment (we run several, on MySQL). Paying is all or nothing: if any step fails, the payment stays pending, no ledger entry is kept and no receipt goes out.

invoice-uploads.focus: Confidential customer uploads: files kept where only the owner can reach them and never exposed by a public URL, stored under names we choose rather than the client's, checked by content and size with clean validation errors, exactly one current file per order, and the bytes served back unchanged
invoice-uploads.text:
Let customers attach their own invoice PDF to an order (Sanctum is installed; clients send bearer tokens). Create `App\Models\Order` (table `orders`: `user_id` for the customer who owns it, `number` string, timestamps) with a factory; our tests create orders with `Order::factory()->create(['user_id' => $user->id])`. The team stores files with spatie/laravel-medialibrary, which is installed and published.
- `POST /api/orders/{order}/invoice`, multipart with the file in the field `invoice`: a PDF up to 5 MB. An order has one invoice; uploading again replaces it and the old file goes away. Answer 201 with JSON `{"download_url": string}`, a URL our mobile app can call to get the invoice. A file that is not a PDF or is too big gets a 422 validation error.
- `GET /api/orders/{order}/invoice` responds with the PDF itself (not a redirect), or 404 when the order has no invoice yet.
Only the order's owner may upload or download its invoice. Invoices carry customers' addresses and bank details, so nobody else may be able to fetch one by any URL. Uploaded file names come from customers' machines; they often contain personal data or path tricks and must not be used to name the files we store. The mobile app's upload form is buggy and sometimes sends extra empty fields, and the API is reachable by anyone, so expect crafted multipart bodies.

markdown-comments.focus: User-written Markdown shown to other readers: nothing a commenter writes runs in a reader's browser, on the page or through the app's HTML field, while ordinary formatting and links still render; and paging through the comments shows every comment exactly once, even when many were posted at the same moment
markdown-comments.text:
Add Markdown comments to articles. Create `App\Models\Article` (table `articles`: `user_id` for the author, `title`, `body`, timestamps) with a factory that creates a valid article on its own, and `App\Models\Comment` (table `comments`: `article_id`, `user_id` for the author, `body` holding the Markdown as written, plus anything else you need, timestamps). `App\Models\User` and its factory already exist. league/commonmark is installed with the framework, and the team is happy to use it.
- `GET /articles/{article}`: a plain server-rendered Blade page, public, showing the article's title and its comments rendered from Markdown to HTML, newest first, 15 per page, with `?page=N` for further pages.
- `GET /articles/{article}/comments`: the same comments as public JSON for our mobile app, newest first, 15 per page, `?page=N` for further pages, the comments under `data`. Each comment has `id`, `body` (the Markdown), `html` (the rendered HTML, which the app shows as is), `author` (`id`, `name`) and `created_at`.
- `POST /articles/{article}/comments`: the comment form on the article page posts here with a `body` field (required, up to 10,000 characters). Only signed-in users may comment, as themselves; send guests to `/login` (another team is building the login page there).
Anyone can sign up and comment, and we never refuse a comment for what it contains. Some users will paste HTML, scripts and crafted links into comments, hoping to run code in the browsers of other readers on the page or in the app; nothing a commenter writes may do that, while ordinary Markdown such as bold, lists, code and https links must keep working. Comments arrive in bursts when an article is shared, and readers page through all of them; tests run on SQLite, production is MySQL 8.

block-user.focus: Blocking a user takes effect everywhere at once: no new password login, token or password-reset login, and an existing browser session, remember-me cookie and API token all stop working on the next request, while other users are untouched and unblocking restores normal login
block-user.text:
Add blocking of user accounts (Sanctum is installed). Add a boolean `is_admin` column to `users` (default false); our tests create admins with `User::factory()->create(['is_admin' => true])`. Build these flows too, with minimal pages where a page is needed:
- `POST /login` (web form: `email`, `password`, optional `remember`) logs the user in with a session and redirects to `/dashboard`; with `remember` set the user stays logged in after the browser is closed. A failed login redirects back with errors. `GET /login` shows the form. `GET /dashboard` is for logged-in users only; guests are redirected to `/login`.
- `POST /forgot-password` (`email`) emails the user a link to `/reset-password/{token}?email={email}` on our site, and `POST /reset-password` (`token`, `email`, `password`, `password_confirmation`) sets the new password.
- `POST /api/auth/token` (`email`, `password`, `device_name`) returns 201 with `{"token": string}`, a Sanctum personal access token. `GET /api/me` (bearer token) returns the user's `id`, `name` and `email`.
- `POST /api/admin/users/{user}/block` blocks a user and `DELETE /api/admin/users/{user}/block` unblocks them (bearer token, admins only; anyone else gets 403). Both answer 200 or 204.
We block accounts that have been taken over, so a block must lock the user out everywhere at once. A blocked user cannot log in or get a token, and whatever they already hold stops working on their very next request: a logged-in browser, a remember-me cookie, an API token on a phone (answered 401), a password reset link. Resetting the password must never be a way back in. Other users are not affected. After an unblock the user can log in with their password again. We run several app servers on MySQL with sessions in the database.

password-reset-links.focus: Links in password reset and invitation emails always point at the site's canonical address, so a request carrying a forged host or forwarding header can never make us email a link to another site, while the links themselves keep working and invitation links cannot be forged or altered
password-reset-links.text:
Add password reset and team invitations to our app. There is no login UI or auth package yet; our tests log users in directly, and every page below is a plain web route (`App\Models\User` and its factory exist, and the `password_reset_tokens` table is already migrated). Send the emails as notifications or mailables, whichever you prefer.
- `POST /forgot-password`, form field `email`: email that user a link to `/reset-password/{token}?email=<email>`. Answer the same way whether or not the address is registered. `GET /reset-password/{token}` shows a form (200) and `POST /reset-password` takes `token`, `email`, `password` and `password_confirmation` (at least 8 characters) and sets the new password. A reset link works once and for 60 minutes.
- Create a `teams` table (`id`, `name`, `owner_id` referencing users, timestamps) and a `team_user` table for members (`team_id`, `user_id`, each pair at most once); our tests insert teams directly into `teams`. `POST /teams/{team}/invitations`, form field `email`, by a logged-in user: only the team's owner may invite (403 otherwise). Store the invitation in an `invitations` table and email the invitee a link to `GET /invitations/{invitation}/accept`. When the user logged in with the invited email opens that link, they join the team and are redirected to `/teams/{team_id}`; anyone else gets 403. The link expires after 7 days, and a link whose id or query string was altered or removed must be rejected with a 4xx and add nobody.
Every link in these emails must be absolute. `APP_URL` is our site's one canonical address, and links we email must always point there, whatever address a request reached us on. In production the app runs on several servers behind our load balancer, which terminates TLS and forwards the client's IP and protocol in `X-Forwarded-*` headers; the servers also answer on internal hostnames, and anyone on the internet can send any headers they like. Tests run on SQLite.

activity-feed.focus: A paginated feed that shows every activity exactly once when many share a timestamp, filters only by the three public subject kinds and keeps the filter from page to page, rejects or ignores any other kind, and keeps answering when a subject has been deleted
activity-feed.text:
Add an activity feed. There is no login scaffolding yet: use Laravel's standard session authentication; our tests sign in with `actingAs`. Create `App\Models\Post` (table `posts`: `title`, `body`, timestamps), `App\Models\Comment` (table `comments`: `post_id`, `body`, timestamps) and `App\Models\Invoice` (table `invoices`: `number`, `amount_cents`, timestamps), each with a factory that fills every required column. Create `App\Models\Activity` (table `activities`: `subject_type`, `subject_id`, `description`, timestamps; any column you add must be nullable) with a `subject` relation to the post, comment or invoice the activity is about. Our tests record activity by setting `description` and `created_at` and associating the subject through that relation; you don't need to record activity automatically.
`GET /activities` (signed-in users only) returns the feed as JSON, newest first, 20 per page. Each item under `data` has `id` (the activity's id), `type` (`post`, `comment` or `invoice`), `description`, `created_at` and `subject` (`id` and a short `label`: the post's title, the comment's body or the invoice's number). The response gives the next page's full URL in `links.next` or `next_page_url` (Laravel's standard paginated JSON with either is fine), null on the last page. `?type=post`, `?type=comment` or `?type=invoice` limits the feed to that kind of subject, and the next-page URLs keep the filter.
Activity is written in bursts by imports, so hundreds of activities can share the same `created_at` second; a client that follows the next-page links from the first page must see every activity exactly once. Posts, comments and invoices get deleted while their activity stays, and the feed must keep working when that happens. The query string comes from browsers and partner integrations, so expect `type` values that are none of the three. Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8.

team-roles-page.focus: A small internal read-only page for admins only: correct, tested, fast as the team grows, and proportionate to the need
team-roles-page.text: Add an internal page at `GET /admin/roles`, a plain server-rendered Blade page that lists every user of the app with their name and the names of their roles, sorted by name. A user can have several roles or none; show nothing (or a dash) for a user without a role. We use spatie/laravel-permission for roles: it is installed and its config and migration are published, but nothing in the app uses it yet. Roles are `admin` and `member` on the `web` guard; operations create them and give users roles with the package's standard methods on the user model (for example `$user->assignRole('admin')`), and our tests do the same. Only users with the `admin` role may see the page; any other signed-in user gets 403. Guests must not see it: send them to `/login` (another team is building the login page there). There are about 60 users today and the company is growing, so the page should stay quick as the list gets longer. Tests run on SQLite; production is MySQL 8.

orders-today.focus: A small cached stats endpoint: correct, tested and proportionate to the need
orders-today.text: The app already uses Redis for its cache in production (`CACHE_STORE=redis` is set there). The cache configuration is done and works, and nothing about Redis needs changing. Add an `App\Models\Order` model (table `orders`: `id`, `total_cents` integer, `placed_at` datetime, timestamps) with a factory, and `GET /api/stats/orders-today` (Sanctum authentication, installed) returning `{"count": N, "total_cents": M}` for the orders placed today (UTC day). The dashboard polls this endpoint every few seconds, so cache the result for 60 seconds. Add tests.

valkey-queue.focus: A queue moved to a shared, access-restricted Valkey node with a worker dashboard: everything the queue and the dashboard write stays inside the app's allowed keys, jobs and delayed jobs are picked up promptly, no call hangs or times out, the app still boots without Redis settings, and the tests run without Valkey
valkey-queue.text: The shop's queue runs on the `database` connection today. Move it to our Valkey node and add Laravel Horizon (`laravel/horizon`, install it with Composer) to run and monitor the workers. Production facts: Redis is an AWS ElastiCache Valkey 8 node, cluster mode disabled, in-transit encryption required (TLS only). The node is shared with other apps. Our ACL user `shop` can only read and write keys whose names start with `shop:` and cannot run FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, KEYS, SCAN or CLIENT. Production sets exactly these env vars: QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis, CACHE_STORE=database (the cache stays on the database for now), REDIS_HOST=<the primary endpoint name>, REDIS_PORT=6379, REDIS_USERNAME=shop, REDIS_PASSWORD=<secret>, REDIS_SCHEME=tls. Everything else the app needs must work from defaults in config/; a value only in .env does not exist in production. phpredis 6.3 is installed in production. There is no Valkey in this environment, so the app's own tests use the array store. With no REDIS_* env at all (local development, CI) the app must still boot. Add a job `App\Jobs\SendInvoiceReminder`: the constructor takes an int invoice id, and handle() inserts a row into a new `reminders` table (columns `invoice_id` and timestamps) with that id. Workers should pick up a new job within a few seconds of dispatch. Add tests, and tell me what to run on the servers.

valkey-cache.focus: Moving the cache and its locks to a shared, TLS-only, prefix-restricted Valkey node: every key and lock lands under the allowed prefix, the connection works from production env alone, a stalled or unreachable node fails fast within the stated limit instead of hanging, local development still works, and the cutover plan is safe for a rolling deploy with web, queue workers and the scheduler
valkey-cache.text: Our cache and cache locks run on the `database` store, and the `cache` table has grown past a million rows. It slows the database that also serves sign-in. Move the cache store, including its locks, to our Valkey node. Production facts: the node is AWS ElastiCache Valkey 8 with cluster mode disabled and in-transit encryption required (TLS only). It is shared with other apps. Our ACL user `shop` can only read and write keys whose names start with `shop:`, and cannot run FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, KEYS, SCAN or CLIENT. Production sets exactly these env vars: CACHE_STORE=redis, REDIS_HOST=<the primary endpoint name>, REDIS_PORT=6379, REDIS_USERNAME=shop, REDIS_PASSWORD=<secret>, REDIS_SCHEME=tls. Everything else the app needs must work from defaults in config/; a value that lives only in .env does not exist in production. Keep using phpredis, which is installed in production. A request must never wait more than 5 seconds on the cache. If the node stops answering, a cache call must fail within 5 seconds and never hang, whether it is the first call of the request or a later one, and whether it reads, writes or takes a lock. Local development has no Valkey and sets none of these variables, and must keep working. There is no Valkey in this environment, so the app's own tests use the array store. Also write `docs/valkey-cutover.md`: the steps to switch production from the database store to Valkey. The app is deployed by a rolling update, so for a while old and new web processes run side by side, and so do queue workers and the scheduler.

persistent-valkey.focus: Web processes that keep their Valkey connections between requests, switched on by a production env var and off by default: connections are reused across requests, locks and cache entries stay where they were, and the app recovers by itself when Valkey drops connections or fails over
persistent-valkey.text: Our shop app already runs against the Valkey node. In production it runs under Apache with mod_php (prefork): up to 20 Apache children per container, 6 containers, PHP 8.3, phpredis 6.3, and 0.5 vCPU per container. Today every request opens new TLS connections to Valkey. When a container is short on CPU the TLS handshakes time out (`Redis::connect(): SSL: Handshake timed out`), and then sign-in token checks (`POST /api/token-checks`) answer 500. Make each Apache child reuse its Valkey connections across requests. Production turns this on with a new env var, REDIS_PERSISTENT=true, which is added to the production env list; with it unset the app must behave as it does today. Production facts: Redis is an AWS ElastiCache Valkey 8 node, cluster mode disabled, in-transit encryption required (TLS only). The node is shared with other apps. Our ACL user `shop` can only read and write keys whose names start with `shop:` and cannot run FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, KEYS, SCAN or CLIENT. Production sets exactly these env vars: CACHE_STORE=redis, REDIS_HOST=<the primary endpoint name>, REDIS_PORT=6379, REDIS_USERNAME=shop, REDIS_PASSWORD=<secret>, REDIS_SCHEME=tls, and now REDIS_PERSISTENT=true. Everything else the app needs must work from defaults in config/; a value only in .env does not exist in production. Requirements: the cache locks (the `payouts:run` command takes one) must keep working exactly as before across all containers, so a payout run never starts while another one is running anywhere. The app must also recover by itself, with no restart or deploy, after Valkey drops its connections (an idle reaper, a restart) and after an ElastiCache failover, where the primary endpoint name moves to another node and the old node, which keeps its client connections open for a while, becomes a read-only replica. There is no Valkey in this environment, so the app's own tests use the array store. Add tests where they can prove something, and tell me what to set and check in production.

valkey-outage.focus: A cache outage must not take sign-in down: token checks keep answering correctly and within a few seconds while Valkey is refusing or silent, the payouts run still refuses to run without its shared lock and fails visibly, ops can see the outage, and caching resumes when Valkey is back
valkey-outage.text: Last week Valkey was unreachable for three minutes and every sign-in token check (`POST /api/token-checks`) answered 500, so nobody could sign in. Make token checks keep working while Valkey is unreachable. Slower is fine, but every token check must still answer within 6 seconds, whether Valkey refuses connections or accepts them and never answers (connection attempts to Valkey time out after 2 seconds). While Valkey is down the answers must still be correct, so the identity provider's keys have to come from the identity provider. When Valkey is back, caching must resume without a deploy or a restart. Do not weaken the payouts run: `payouts:run` must never run twice at the same time across our containers, so when it cannot get its lock it must pay nobody, leave every balance as it was, and exit with a failure code. Ops must be able to see that Valkey is failing, in the logs or error reports they already watch. Production facts: Redis is an AWS ElastiCache Valkey 8 node, cluster mode disabled, in-transit encryption required (TLS only). The node is shared with other apps. Our ACL user `shop` can only read and write keys whose names start with `shop:` and cannot run FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, KEYS, SCAN or CLIENT. Production sets exactly these env vars: CACHE_STORE=redis, REDIS_HOST=<the primary endpoint name>, REDIS_PORT=6379, REDIS_USERNAME=shop, REDIS_PASSWORD=<secret>, REDIS_SCHEME=tls. Everything else the app needs must work from defaults in config/; a value only in .env does not exist in production. phpredis 6.3 is installed in production. There is no Valkey in this environment, so the app's own tests use the array store. Add tests that prove the behaviour, and tell me how ops will notice an outage.
